member of the commission.– madam president, today we are discussing the introduction of the new emissions testing procedures for cars in the eu. as you know, we have been working on this issue for quite a long time, but of course the volkswagen revelations gave action greater urgency. so i want to focus today’s debate on the impact of the decision that has been taken. we know that laboratory tests are not reliable. currently, the real nox emissions by diesel cars are, on average, 400 mg/km. that is 4-5 times higher than the legal emissions limit of euro 6 cars. that is why we have prepared some substantial changes to the regulatory framework. of course, it was demanding, but we have come up with a solution that is unique and fit for purpose. we will be the first in the world to introduce emissions tests on real roads under real driving conditions. our solutions will change the current measurement systems completely. it will no longer be possible to cheat in emissions tests. member states have reached a compromise. in the first stage emissions will be reduced to 168 mg/km by september next year and then, by january 2020, the limits will be reduced still further to 120 mg/km. you are well aware that the initial commission proposals were significantly more ambitious. i said on many occasions that i wanted more stringent ‘conformity factors’, but we could not convince the member states. still – and i want to underline this – i consider this agreement substantial progress because we are halving the nox emissions of diesel cars currently on the streets and, at the same time, we are forcing the automotive industry to speed up efforts to make cars cleaner and respect our common environmental goals. this is why we need the new rules as soon as possible, and this is why we need – and ask for – your agreement on the commission’s proposals on introducing real driving emissions tests in the eu. but, as i have also told you, we will not stop here. the real driving emissions tests are only one part of the package. we want to bring down nox emissions as much as possible. ultimately, if technological development allows, we want the cars to achieve the legal limit of 80 mg/km. that is why the legal proposal on the real driving emissions test procedures suggests a so-called annual revision clause. this means that, from 2020 onwards, the emission limits can be adjusted if technology improves. each year, the commission will assess the portable measurements technology: this is the technology which actually measures the emissions under real driving conditions. if this technology improves and allows for more exact emission measurements from 2020, we will have the legal possibility to bring the limits down further, to 80 mg/km. we intend to start this work already by the end of this year. it is possible to do so within this time limit because manufacturers design their vehicles well in advance of their production, so the vehicles on the roads in five years’ time are being designed today. that is why the existence of the annual revision clause provides legal certainty and an incentive for car manufacturers to design their cars with much lower emissions than the current limit. let me now come to the rest of the package. in the course of this year, the commission will propose a third regulatory package on real driving emissions testing to increase transparency. the idea is that the conformity factor of each vehicle is shown in its certificate of conformity: the consumer will be fully aware of the emissions performance of his/her vehicle. further, i promised to improve the type approval system and strengthen the independence of the control bodies. i will propose the text for the college discussion next week. the new rules will clarify and strengthen the recall system and safeguard procedures. the commission will be given the powers to intervene and comment on the corrective measures taken by the member states. the system of exchange of information and cooperation between enforcement authorities in the member states will be reinforced. the volkswagen case also showed that member states do not react in a very coordinated manner, so i intend to force member states to carry out market surveillance and controls of vehicles brought to the market. the quality and independence of the services responsible for approving vehicles will be strengthened. this means more quality checks, better cooperation and more and stronger tools to enforce the rules. we need to restore the confidence of our citizens in the type approval system and the car industry as a whole, as we have all agreed a few times before. this is why we urgently need new rules on type approval and emissions testing to be in place. last, but not least, a few words about euro 5/6 proposals: the parliament and council are currently negotiating some revisions of the euro 5 and euro 6 legislation, which is also the parent legislation to the act on introducing real driving emissions. in this context, the delegated powers to be given to the commission are being discussed. our objective is to have a very smooth and rapid implementation of the new real driving emissions procedure in the future. we are ready to work together with you, and of course with the council, to find a balanced solution because we want to achieve our environmental objectives and we are determined to respect the institutional balance. i know this is also important to you. i hope that my commitment is very clear to you. i want to tackle it in a very coherent and comprehensive way. i will be demanding and decisive towards our car manufacturers if they do not play the game. i am confident that this new framework will restore the effectiveness of our legal system to protect both consumers and the environment.
on behalf of the ppe group what's at stake here? we all know that. we want to reduce harmful nitrogen oxide emissions effectively and as quickly as possible. today - and the commissioner has just confirmed it - a euro 6 diesel car emits on average four times more nitrogen than the legal standard we adopted a few years ago and which came into force last year. so we need to reduce those emissions. we all agree on that. secondly: the new test, the real driving emission test, which determines how much cars emit in real driving conditions, must now finally be introduced. there is an agreement on that, and that is essential. we've wasted enough time. that test needs to be entered now. we welcome, of course, commissioner, that you are here pledging to come forward in the short term with a legislative proposal on additional supervision of national typeapproval, on that typeapproval. it is essential that national controls can be independently and robustly verified. i also refer to the debate on delegated and implementing acts. parliament wants to be directly involved in future revisions. we are asking for this to be done by means of delegated acts and not by means of implementing acts. and finally , this: smart car manufacturers, of course, don't wait to react. they are taking the leap and starting today to adapt their cars using the smartest technology for the benefit of the public health of everyone in europe. the speaker is prepared to answer a 'blue card' question (rule 162 (8)).
"blue card" is the answer. i don't know if that's very relevant here. the most important thing today is that we draw conclusions as quickly as possible from the situation that has arisen and from the scandals that have occurred. what is important is, first, that the nitrous oxide goes down as quickly as possible. we have a commission of inquiry to find out what went wrong. one of the conclusions will undoubtedly be that the control of type-approval must be tightened up, that there must be an independent and robust control of type-approval. we need to focus on what went wrong. that will be apparent during the work of the committee of inquiry. we must now concentrate on the question of how to get nitrous oxide down in the interest of the public health of all of us and the sooner the better. in writing. i welcome the adoption by the european parliament of its position on the proposal for a regulation on a multiannual plan for the recovery of tuna stocks in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean. the purpose of this regulation is to incorporate into union law the recommendations of the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas, which aim to ensure the conservation of tuna stocks and thus the sustainability of fishing opportunities. the recommendations in this report take account of the positive evolution of tuna stocks in recent years, which is the result of management measures to ensure the sustainability of these stocks. the incorporation of such measures decided at international level into union law is a crucial step towards their uniform application at european level and thus ensuring the coherence of the common fisheries policy. i also support parliament's request to preserve the powers of our assembly to transpose into union law measures decided in the international bodies for the management of fisheries activities.

in writing. ‒ the n-va delegation in the european parliament supports this evaluation report on eu legislation in the field of financial services. we are less enthusiastic, however, about the fact that the report mentions the 'great steps' taken by the entry into force of the solvency ii directive. the n-va meps abstained on the part of the text referring to solvency ii. investments by insurers with a guarantee from the federal government are given a more favourable risk weight than investments backed by a flemish regional guarantee. this distinction, which imposes additional capital costs on flemish insurers, is indefensible. the european union is making an unfair abstraction from the belgian institutional system. a flemish guarantee should be weighed in the same way as a guarantee from the federal government. moreover, for direct exposures this distinction is not made. this provision should therefore be updated. as soon as possible. we therefore continue to raise this issue in the european parliament and in the european commission.
in writing. the financial crisis of 2007-2008 gave rise to an ambitious programme of reform of the union's financial sector. the time has now come to take stock of the new framework and assess its adequacy to the challenges of the present. we must ensure financial stability which ensures growth in investment, mainly in the long term. financial markets need to respond better to the financing needs of the real economy. however, in this report we have stressed the increasing complexity of the legislation. it is therefore essential that we have a global vision in order to maintain consistency in the european regulations in force.
in writing. ‒ in 2008, the financial crisis known as the subprime mortgage crisis in the us was sweeping across europe, severely and permanently weakening the european economy. we must remember the high cost and the considerable effort required of taxpayers to help the banking sector: 26% of european gdp was absorbed in this task. since then, the european union has certainly spared no effort to stabilise the financial system, and in particular the banking system, and many pieces of legislation have been adopted in the last three years: a single resolution mechanism in the event of bank failures, a framework for managing bank failures and a deposit guarantee system. so it's time for the mid-course countdown. the european parliament called on the commission on tuesday to carry out an impact study of the 40 pieces of eu legislation on the financial market that have been implemented since the crisis. the aim is to be able to judge the consistency and proportionality of the rules while identifying any undesirable side effects that would weaken smes and investors.
in writing. ‒ the financial and debt crisis of 2007/2008 required comprehensive action by european legislators. since then, numerous legislative initiatives in the area of financial services have been launched with a view to restoring financial stability, strengthening consumer protection and implementing the lessons learned from the crisis. the aim of this own-initiative report, which was voted on yesterday, is to take an initial look at this legislative work, to address the shortcomings in the financial services legislation and to express concern that the effects of the various legislative measures have not been sufficiently analysed so far. however, a thorough assessment of the effects of the financial services framework is necessary and should be repeated regularly. moreover, the application of financial services legislation should be made more comprehensible and better adapted to the needs of smes. financial stability and consumer protection must remain the priorities of policymakers, with greater emphasis on the implementation of a coherent risk-based strategy.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the text on the balance sheet and the challenges of eu regulation of financial services, even though i would have liked to go further. i see that the financial and debt crisis we are going through has had unprecedented consequences, particularly on the real economy and on taxpayers' money. i therefore welcome the financial regulation approved by the european institutions over the last five years, which has strengthened europe's financial architecture in preparation for future crises. we have got the commission to include an effective level of consumer and investor protection, which is one of the founding principles of this union.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which gives us a broader view of the state of play of legislative measures relating to financial markets. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the rules on capital markets are fully applied.
in writing. ‒ given the importance of entrepreneurship in creating jobs and the fact that women accounted for only 31% of entrepreneurs in the european union in 2012, i have endorsed this report which calls on member states to adopt concrete strategies to remove obstacles to female entrepreneurship. this is an integral part of gender equality, which must be one of our key political priorities. this includes a better work-life balance for all, support for women's entrepreneurship, access to finance and the creation and support for the development of networks.
in writing. since the launch of the lisbon treaty, promoting entrepreneurship has been a political priority for europe. to make our economy more efficient and to create more new jobs, we need more entrepreneurs. yet we still find that entrepreneurship in europe lags behind the other major economies in the world. while in the us 21% of the population opts for entrepreneurship, in europe only 12% of the active population opts for self-employment. of all the selfemployed and entrepreneurs in europe, it is found that only 31% are women. women are more likely to choose to work as employees, even if this is to maintain a balance between their private and professional lives. the report makes a strong case for removing the obstacles that potential female entrepreneurs still face. all too often, women entrepreneurs rely on financial support from family and acquaintances. access to credit lines for women entrepreneurs should therefore be facilitated. i also fully support the measures proposed to eliminate stereotypes about female entrepreneurship and to promote female entrepreneurship through training and study options.
in writing. ‒ in europe, women account for only 31% of entrepreneurs and are most often in sectors considered less profitable: education, healthcare and social work. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. the means envisaged to achieve this are many: the promotion of an entrepreneurial culture within our societies or the establishment of support structures to facilitate the reconciliation of work and family life for women. women are twice as likely as men to work part-time. all these proposals are moving in the right direction. however, i do not think that quotas are the best solution, and the debate on paternity leave is certainly not a european priority, given the difficulty of reaching agreement between member states on this issue. women's entrepreneurship in europe is nevertheless an important societal issue that foreshadows the advent of a more liberal, less codified and rigid western society, which gives priority to individual initiative.
in writing. ‒ yesterday, in plenary, the european parliament looked at the reasons why women are generally less likely to set out as self-employed than men. a report was voted calling on the european commission and the member states to take up the matter and encourage women to become entrepreneurs. in europe, women are twice as likely as men to choose self-employment, accounting for only 31% of self-employed persons in the 28 eu member states in 2012. the text of the report reviews the obstacles which prevent women from becoming entrepreneurs. for example, women have a harder time accessing traditional equity financing, and they tend to start their businesses with less capital and smaller loans. the text adopted calls on the member states and the european commission to promote an entrepreneurial culture from the very beginning of girls' education and to consider instruments - including financial instruments - to help women to start their own businesses.
in writing. ‒ the n-va delegation in the european parliament abstained from voting on this report. the n-va is a strong supporter of equal opportunities for men and women and is working towards a strong, coordinated policy on equal opportunities. in abstaining, the n-va delegation wishes to point out in particular that (1) we do not agree with the recommendation to the commission to introduce gender quotas for any aid to underrepresented and disadvantaged groups; (2) the report is excessively intrusive on matters of the private sphere; (3) and the language used in certain paragraphs is very woman-friendly.
in writing. - i'm on the same page as mrs. matera. we call on the eu institutions, the member states and regional and local authorities to take more active action, including concrete measures, to combat the stereotypes about the respective characteristics and abilities of women and men that persist in sectors where men are in the majority, such as science and technology, or innovation and invention. in these sectors, women are likely to be perceived as less credible or less professional than men by decision-makers, investors, the financial sector and the market, which means that women entrepreneurs are sometimes viewed with skepticism by potential customers, suppliers, partners, banks and investors, and that they must demonstrate much greater tenacity to prove their knowledge, skills and abilities, and to be able to access the funding they need.
in writing. ‒ as a female politician and a champion of women's rights, this issue is close to my heart. in europe, women represent only 31% of all entrepreneurs, and they are even more prevalent in the softer sectors such as health, education and social work. this has been made clearer in recent days by the under-representation of women in davos. i approved this report on the external factors that hinder female entrepreneurship because i want to encourage the european commission to promote female entrepreneurship in all sectors.
in writing. ‒ currently, more than 7 million young people aged 15-24 are not in employment, education or training. for many of them, victims of the banking and business crisis, the lack of skills is a structural barrier to accessing sustainable employment that will enable them to pursue a life project. i am deeply involved in the fight for jobs for farciennes and i see every day the human consequences that this can have. i therefore naturally supported this report which stresses that the development of individual skills and the dissemination of knowledge and skills are one of the aspects of integrated social and employment policies. it is clear that schools, training bodies and, of course, companies must make this struggle for employment a priority. but the overall socioeconomic context is also essential. the commission has launched the youth guarantee, which should be highlighted. but it cannot take back what it has given from one hand and must commit itself to a genuine investment-based recovery policy which will reduce unemployment and poverty and finally give prospects for the future to millions of young europeans.
tackling youth unemployment remains one of the greatest challenges in europe. despite the fact that more than 7 million young people were unemployed in europe at the end of 2014, we also find that 2 million vacancies are not being filled. it is therefore of the utmost importance that europe and the member states take initiatives to get more young people into work. an integrated employment policy means anticipating labour market developments more quickly and matching individual skills development with specific labour market demands. it is also advisable to intensify cooperation between educational institutions and economic sectors in the context of cross-sectoral cooperation. i also support the recommendation in this report to intensify the eures european job network and labour mobility so that, especially in border regions, young people are encouraged to take up cross-border job offers. finally, it is also recommended that extra efforts be made to promote entrepreneurship among young people. in this context, it is appropriate that all member states engage in the erasmus programme for young entrepreneurs.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament backed a key report this afternoon to combat youth unemployment. in november 2015, according to eurostat, 20% of young europeans aged 15-24 were unemployed (27.8% in brussels). nearly 5 million young people are unemployed, while 2 million jobs remain open. with a budget of 6 billion, the union must take action to combat this problem, which affects economic development and social cohesion throughout its territory. i have of course supported this essential report which emphasizes greater flexibility in education systems in the face of a constantly changing labour market, in order to ensure a better match between the knowledge acquired and the skills needed for the labour market. here again, and it is not for lack of repetition, education must work in tandem with business to combat this scourge effectively. a small step has been taken, but there is still a long way to go.
in writing. ‒ vocational and flexible education, non-formal and innovative learning, workplace training, traineeships and mobility are all tools that member states should strengthen to better develop the individual skills of young europeans. this approach is contained in the resolution on 'policies to promote skills development to combat youth unemployment', which was adopted yesterday in plenary in strasbourg. the main message of the text, which has received wide support, is that today more bridges must be built between the world of education, which must be modernised (new teaching methods), and that of business, which must be supported by public authorities (regional, national and european). the aim is to facilitate the integration into the labour market of the five million unemployed young people aged 15 to 24 in the union and the seven million young europeans who are not in employment, education or training.
in writing. ‒ this report highlights the importance of focusing on the skills of young people in the fight against youth unemployment. of course, this is of great importance, but it is not a panacea. we will not solve youth unemployment by just focusing on skills. green amendments have ensured that this report now also focuses on the problem of structural unemployment. we must increase the supply of quality jobs and create structural and sustainable jobs for all. education not only prepares young people for the labour market, but is also very important for the personal development of young people. this may lead to finding a suitable job. every youngster is different. this should be taken into account when learning skills. social actors must be supported in providing training and job creation. we must be bold enough to invest in sectors with a future, especially in clean technology and green jobs. and we need to give young start-ups and smes a boost so that they can develop their own initiatives. equal opportunities are also important, especially for people with disabilities. because everyone should be able to develop his or her skills to the full, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ this text provides an opportunity to recall the essential role of enterprises, in particular smes, social and solidarity economy actors and microenterprises, in vocational skills training and job creation for young people. we must emphasise the need to provide young people with an education which introduces them to the spirit of enterprise in the broadest possible way. we must advocate that training programmes include the development, in a safe environment, of the professional skills necessary for the creation and management of enterprises, and that transversal entrepreneurial skills, abilities and knowledge are promoted which are effectively acquired through practical and real-life experience.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on skills-based policies to combat youth unemployment in the european union. in europe, on the one hand, we have 4.5 million young people without a job and, on the other, 2 million unfilled vacancies. measures are therefore needed to bridge this gap. the european parliament has already expressed its views on the commission's proposal.
in writing. ‒ this report welcomes the commission communication 'a strategy for a digital single market in europe' as it believes that the creation of such a market, based on a set of rules, could have a positive influence on growth and employment and make society more inclusive. for example, e-commerce generates 500 billion euros a year in the european union! however, it must be kept in mind that it is important to think at every stage about the inclusion of the most vulnerable citizens. they cannot remain on the margins of a digital society that has too often developed without them. the social divide would only grow. the commission will also be looking at consumer protection, the protection of personal data and the fight against illegal content on the net.
in writing. europe must join the digital train as soon as possible, as it affects all aspects of the lives of citizens, young people, public figures and businessmen, and even changes democracy itself. the digital economy is a mine of job creation, innovation and growth. we're making a technological leap by combining machines, networks, telecommunications and computing. however, it cannot be achieved without respect for data protection and privacy. while every european citizen has the right to the internet and broadband wherever they are, they also have the right to respect for their privacy. i am therefore in favour of a regulated digital single market which puts the individual at the centre of its concerns.
in writing. ‒ end of geo-blocking, which prevents watching news or football matches streamed from abroad on the websites of national channels, and end of being prevented from watching the podcast of foreign tv shows. this is in any case the intention of the european parliament, which on tuesday called for the rapid implementation of a digital single market based on 16 proposals made by the commission in may 2015. among the latter, i would mention first of all the desire to achieve rapidly widespread coverage of the 4g network, which currently covers only 15% of europeans in rural areas, in accordance with the principle of universal access. other measures are also urgent: the removal of geo-blocking and its ip-based restrictions, the reduction of delivery charges in transnational e-commerce to boost online sales. it will of course take a few years for all this to become a reality, but this promising digital revolution will allow europe, if it makes the right choices and quickly, to generate €415 billion of additional wealth every year and to enter the 21st century cognitive society on its feet.
in writing. ‒ this non-legislative resolution adopted yesterday is parliament's response to the roadmap presented by the commission in may 2015. the text is based on two key objectives: first, to improve access to the digital single market for consumers and businesses across europe; and second, to create an enabling environment and fair conditions of competition for innovative services and advanced digital networks. it also pursues more transversal objectives, such as asking the commission to launch a study on the side effects of digitalisation (i.e. on the development of children's cognitive abilities). but it ignores the most controversial issues, such as the impossibility of reconciling the principle of the territoriality of copyright and the end of geographical blocking. finally, i supported an amendment which states that the commission and all member states must strictly uphold the principle of net neutrality and which calls on the commission to preserve the openness of the internet as a global platform for communication, production, participation, creation, cultural diversity and innovation, in the interests of citizens, consumers and the success of european businesses as a whole.
in writing. ‒ we want to improve european consumers' access to online goods and services, eliminate differences in treatment between offline and online purchases, and eliminate discrimination linked to geo-blocking. so many obstacles remain for smes and consumers, explaining the grim figures for online commerce in europe. while only 4% of european online transactions are cross-border (compared to 42% of national transactions and 54% from the us), 45% of european households do not have high-speed internet! an effective digital market is urgently needed for the economy, employment and social inclusion.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this act because it can promote the competitiveness of the european union as a whole and will give a new impetus to our internal market. we need an open market: this is the only way to respond successfully to the digitisation of the economy.

member of the commission.– madam president, first i would like to thank the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and congratulate the rapporteurs ms ford, ms stihler and mr lópez-istúriz white for their hard work on the three files, which made it possible to find a satisfactory compromise which will, hopefully, help us to swiftly adopt the three regulations at first reading. a thorough and deeper single market is one of the priorities of the commission. this package demonstrates that we are also not falling short on delivery. it is an important step in assuring a simpler legal framework. the three regulations on personal protective equipment, gas appliances and cableway installations cover a significant part of the products circulating in our internal market. they concern a vast range of products which millions of eu citizens use on a daily basis. it is crucial that single market legislation ensures that these products are safe and, of course, as regards personal protective equipment in particular, that this actually provides adequate protection. we also need to ensure that the companies producing those products can count on the legal framework that meets their needs and allows them to be competitive and prosper: a legal framework that is clear and does not impose an excessive burden. this package is really a major step forward in our endeavour to simplify the regulatory environment as the so-called ‘new approach’ directives are changed into regulations, which will be directly applicable in every eu member state. this will significantly facilitate the life of enterprises. instead of analysing and researching 28 national transposition laws, companies can directly refer to one single text available in all official languages of the european union. with the adoption of the package we are also a step closer to completing the implementation of the new legislative framework, which will make the whole of our single market legislation much more consistent and easier to apply. new obligations have been introduced for importers and distributors, who now have a very clear set of tasks and checks that they must carry out before importing products from third countries into the eu. new rules on traceability will make it possible to follow a product throughout the entire distribution chain. the package will also give better tools to market surveillance authorities, allowing them to fight more efficiently against unsafe and non-compliant products on the eu market. this will be to the benefit of all companies, making them comply with the applicable rules. it will also reduce unfair competition. the benefits of this package are for all: for consumers, enterprises and authorities. and they are clearly there. let me make one short remark on an institutional issue. it must be clear – and the recently-concluded negotiations on the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making have confirmed this – that comitology committees are not the same as commission expert groups. with the new interinstitutional agreement coming into place shortly, the commission will play closer attention to the role of the committees. the adoption of these proposals will doubtless have a positive effect on entrepreneurship and competitiveness in europe. thus, considering the agreement that has been achieved by the co-legislators and the benefits and significant added value for enterprises, citizens and national administrations, as i illustrated previously, the commission welcomes the agreed compromise package. commission's statements on:1. report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on cableway installations [com(2014)0187 - c7-0111/2014 - 2014/0107(cod)] - committee on the internal market and consumer protection. rapporteur: antonio lópez-istúriz white (a8-0063/2015) “with regard to recital 65 and the possibility of the european parliament to be invited to meetings of expert groups, the commission will implement this recital in accordance with its practice in the implementation of point 15 of the framework agreement on relations between the european parliament and the european commission. meetings of the comitology committee are explicitly excluded under this arrangement. concerning the reference to infringements in the same recital, the commission considers this misleading as infringements proceeding are discussed with member states in the context of the procedures set out under article 258 tfeu.” "the commission regrets the adoption of article 44(5) and recital 64 that creates confusion and legal uncertainty, and may compromise institutional balance. the role of the comitology committees which ensure control by member states on the commission's exercise of implementing powers is defined only by regulation no (eu) 182/2011, adopted on the basis of article 291, third paragraph, tfeu. therefore, no other secondary legislative act can alter or would need to specify further this role. in particular, the comitology committees should not perform the functions which are those of the commission's groups of experts. in addition, the rules of procedures of committees are adopted by the committees on the basis of regulation no (eu) 182/2011. as such they are to be applied when the committee exercises its role defined by regulation no (eu) 182/2011. any reference to rules of procedures outside this context is superfluous and inappropriate. it also risks complicating the functioning of the committee." 2. report on the proposal for a i am speaking on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i am speaking to you as the epp negotiator on this proposal for a regulation on personal protective equipment. the european single market is characterised by high standards of consumer protection worldwide. i would even say and argue that nowhere is a consumer protected as well as in or by the eu. in particular, this regulation sets very high standards for helmets, ear protectors, bicycle helmets, sunglasses and safety vests. it's not about the self-hooked pot lids, it's not about the dishwasher gloves. this regulation therefore concerns each and every one of us. when i buy my little daughter a bicycle helmet, when my father, as a home-maker, puts on a respirator or when countless workers put on a helmet on a construction site, then everyone must be able to count on optimal protection being guaranteed - and this throughout europe. we therefore need high binding standards to protect consumers from products of poor quality. the european parliament has also been asked to give its opinion on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive. so what good are the best rules if nobody is able to implement them? i am particularly pleased that we have agreed on a simplified recertification procedure. this means that if a manufacturer does not change anything about the product and the product still complies with all the legal requirements, then he should not have to pay for this authorisation again. so here we can show that we can do both. on the one hand, to protect consumers throughout europe effectively against fraud and poor quality, and on the other hand, to do away with excessive bureaucratic requirements. i therefore strongly and explicitly call for support for this report.

in writing. ‒ this legislative report concerns the commission's proposal to guarantee a minimum level of protection of the principle of the presumption of innocence in all member states and to strengthen the right of accused persons to be present at their trial. the main elements are the presumption of innocence, the burden of proof, the right not to incriminate oneself, the right not to cooperate and the right to be present at the trial. the rapporteur has amended this proposal to strengthen its protective character for citizens, in particular with regard to the impossibility of reversing the burden of proof to the detriment of suspects, the inadmissibility of evidence obtained in breach of the principle of the presumption of innocence and the extent of the presumption of innocence. at a time when certain european governments are putting fundamental rights at risk, i have of course supported this report.
in writing. i am pleased that the european parliament has adopted this legislation which aims to strengthen a right as fundamental as the presumption of innocence in criminal proceedings. justice can only be virtuous if it effectively guarantees the basic principle of considering a person innocent as long as he has not been found guilty. it was a priority for the european parliament to ensure that the burden of proof was not reversed in any case. this implies that any doubt as to the question of guilt is to the advantage of the accused. the text also recalls a series of rights linked to the right to the presumption of innocence, such as the right to remain silent, the right not to incriminate oneself or the right to be present at trial.
in writing. ‒ the presumption of innocence is a fundamental right of citizens to avoid arbitrary decisions during criminal proceedings. this is what meps have been reminding us of this afternoon when they adopted by a very large majority (577 votes in favour) the new directive on the presumption of innocence negotiated by my friend nathalie griesbeck for the european parliament. the new european legislation is obviously not intended to interfere with the organisation of judicial systems and criminal proceedings by public authorities, which remain the prerogative of the member states, but to set minimum standards for fair trials throughout the european union. despite the existence of national legislation on the presumption of innocence, many violations of this principle still persist in europe. this is why this european directive is important in that it harmonises essential aspects of the presumption of innocence, such as the right not to be accused by public authorities before a trial or the conditions for the admissibility of evidence.
in writing. ‒ we adopted the draft agreement reached last november between the european parliament and the council of the european union on the directive on the presumption of innocence. this directive is to ensure that the principle of the presumption of innocence is applied throughout the union and member states will have to act accordingly until the guilt of the suspect has been proven, for example by avoiding handcuffing him unless these measures are strictly necessary. the text adopted recognises that the burden of proof should rest with the prosecutors and that any doubt raised should benefit the accused. furthermore, the right to remain silent should not be used against individuals. once formally adopted by the council, member states will have two years to transpose this text.
in writing. ‒ the main elements of the proposal therefore relate to the principle of the presumption of innocence, the burden of proof, the right not to incriminate oneself and not to cooperate, the right to remain silent, the right to be present at one's trial and the right to a retrial. it's a good report and i voted for it.
in writing. ‒ the presumption of innocence is one of the most fundamental principles of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. judging in criminal proceedings is a delicate and dangerous undertaking: can and should never be an option. the damage of a miscarriage of justice in criminal proceedings is immense, and its impact can ruin the rest of a person's life. this new directive therefore aims to ensure that the presumption of innocence in criminal cases is better respected throughout the eu.
in writing. ‒ i have approved this report, which aims to extend the scope of the current personal protective equipment directive (any device or means intended to be worn or held by a person to protect him or her against one or more risks to life or health) in order to better protect the health and safety of users of ppe. in particular, it removes the exclusions for products for private use providing protection against heat, moisture and water.
in writing. support for this regulation is intended to ensure the safety of certain protective clothing such as life jackets, bicycle helmets and sunglasses. the amendments are essential for legislation adapted to the products of the 21st century. consumer protection is not just about ensuring that the right price is paid, but also about ensuring that the product you buy is safe and of good quality. i support this regulation, which follows on from the interinstitutional agreement of 22 september last, which ensures the safety of products in a globalised world, and which does not hinder the market, by allowing manufacturers to benefit from a simplified procedure for renewing their certificates of conformity with health and safety rules.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this proposal for a regulation which aims to modernise the current, often confusing, regulatory framework.
in writing. ‒ i have approved this report, which supports the proposal for a regulation to simplify and harmonise european legislation on the internal market for gas appliances by enhancing consumer safety and the rational use of energy.
in writing. the adoption of this regulation is primarily aimed at ensuring that consumers and the professionals concerned are afforded the necessary and identical protection, regardless of where the product is manufactured (gas stove, boiler). it was therefore necessary to introduce obligations both for economic operators and for the national entities responsible for verifying compliance with safety standards. the free movement of goods is one of the cornerstones of the european construction. it requires us to optimise our cooperation and to strengthen our competitiveness. it cannot be done at the expense of consumer protection but must, on the contrary, remain at the service of consumers.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this harmonisation text. the gas sector plays an important role in the union's economy and employs 476 000 people in the gas appliance sector alone. gas appliances cover a wide range of products, from simple gas stoves to boilers in large buildings, and the current stock of gas appliances is 470 million and growing, with more than 30 million units sold each year.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the directive to be transposed into a regulation. this will simplify the rules and national authorities will no longer be able to simply impose additional requirements in their national legislation.
in writing. ‒ i have approved this resolution, which supports the proposal for a regulation to harmonise the conditions for placing on the market of subsystems and safety components for cable installations and to ensure the free movement of products within the union. the proposal requires that all safety components and subsystems be designed and manufactured in accordance with the essential requirements laid down in the proposal for a regulation.
in writing. this proposal for a regulation is the result of an interinstitutional agreement on product safety reached in september 2015 on cable installations (ropeways and cableway installations). it aims to simplify and update the provisions of directive 2000/9/ec with a view to improving legal certainty. replacing a directive with a regulation is an appropriate legal instrument which, by imposing clear and detailed rules, introduces identical obligations for economic operators and national entities responsible for verifying compliance with safety standards. this is the only way to ensure uniform implementation throughout the union.
in writing. - compared to safety devices or gas-fuelled appliances, cable cars may not seem like our frequent companions and one might have doubts about the need for the proposed regulation. but here too, the same rules apply within the single market, and i am convinced that the proposal comes from our committee on the internal market and consumer protection in a rational form that deserves your support.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament yesterday put forward proposals for regulations to improve the safety of certain products. one of these concerns cable infrastructure (cableway, cable cars). the amendments to the regulations proposed by the european parliament will simplify and modernise the legislation in place for 25 years, which aims to prevent counterfeit or fraudulent security products from being placed on the market. those amendments introduce, in particular, certain obligations for economic operators and national entities responsible for verifying compliance with safety standards. manufacturers will also benefit from a simplified procedure for renewing their certificates of conformity with health and safety rules.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this text which deals with the question of the scope of application of directive 2000/9/ec on cable installations. as established in the impact assessment, which was positively assessed by the parliament's ex ante impact assessment unit, a majority of stakeholders cited improving legal clarity as one of the key objectives.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the directive to be transposed into a regulation. this will simplify the rules and ensure their uniform application throughout the european union.

president of the european central bank. – mr president, we are undoubtedly at a point in time when the cohesion of europe is being tested. many of the challenges we must confront are european or even global in nature, and these challenges demand a strong european response. i am therefore grateful to be back in this assembly – a symbol of the need for european debates and european solutions. today we are discussing the annual report of the european central bank for 2014. in that year, the governing council adopted a series of measures to respond to the impairment of our monetary policy transmission channels and to the low inflation environment. these measures included two reductions in key ecb interest rates, the announcement of targeted long-term refinancing operations, and two purchase programmes for asset-backed securities and covered bonds. 2014 was also marked by the start of the activities of the single supervisory mechanism and the completion of the comprehensive assessment. but rather than looking backwards, allow me to focus on the challenges that still lie ahead of us. first, i will briefly explain our current monetary policy and why we will re-assess our stance at our march meeting. second, i would like to discuss the economic challenges we face and what it takes to address them. i am acutely aware that the focus of policymakers lies elsewhere for the moment. but let me be quite clear: economic success is also part of the solution in other fields. therefore, mitigating economic risks deserves to be high on the political agenda. it was about three years ago that inflation started moving away from the ecb’s medium-term inflation aim of below, but close to, 2%. since october 2013, inflation has been below 1%. throughout 2015, headline inflation in the euro area was very low or even negative, remaining under the influence of low commodity prices. euro area annual hicp inflation was estimated at 0.4% in january this year. in parallel to this trend, we had to continually revise our outlook for inflation: while at the start of 2015 our staff was forecasting inflation to reach 1.5% in 2016 and 1.8% in 2017, in december they projected a rate of only 1% for this year, and 1.6% for 2017. against this backdrop, the ecb decided in december to act again. our assessment of the monetary policy stance had two parts. first, we noted that the measures put in place since the summer of 2014 had been very effective. the monetary stimulus that they introduced led to a broad-based easing of financing conditions, stimulated credit provision and has since provided substantial support to the euro area recovery. without these measures, the euro area would have been in outright deflation last year and prices would have fallen at an even quicker pace this year. growth would have been significantly lower. second, while our measures were deemed effective, they were also judged to be insufficient in view of the deteriorating outlook for price stability. there was a concrete risk that without increasing the quantitative stimulus, the date by which inflation would settle around levels below, but close to, 2% would once more be pushed back beyond any relevant definition of medium-term. therefore, we decided to recalibrate our monetary policy stance. we cut the deposit facility rate further to -0.3%; we extended the envisaged end-date for our monthly purchases to the end of march 2017, while maintaining its conditionality on the inflation outlook; and we announced that we would reinvest the principal payments of our purchased assets once they mature, for as long as necessary. we also decided to continue conducting the main refinancing operations and the three-month longer-term refinancing operations as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as necessary, and at least until the end of the last reserve maintenance period of 2017. since our meeting in early december, conditions have once more changed. a moderate recovery of the euro area economy is under way, driven mainly by domestic demand. but downside risks have increased again and there is heightened uncertainty about emerging market economies’ growth prospects, volatility in financial and commodity markets, and geopolitical risks. inflation dynamics are also tangibly weaker than we expected in december. while the most recent wave of disinflation is mainly due to the renewed sharp fall in oil prices, weaker than anticipated growth in wages together with declining inflation expectations call for careful analysis of the channels by which surprises to realised inflation may influence future price and wage-setting in our economy. therefore, at our last meeting in january we judged that it would be necessary to review and possibly reconsider our monetary policy stance at our next monetary policy meeting in early march, when the new staff macroeconomic projections will be made available. our monetary policy is working, and the ecb is willing to contribute its share to ensuring that recovery remains firmly on track. but there are risks that – if they were to materialise – could undermine its course. the policy challenges we face are fourfold. they relate to the global environment, the situation of the financial system, the economic and fiscal policies of member states and the political uncertainty surrounding the european project. first, as regards the global environment: growth prospects are slowly improving in advanced economies, but the outlook in emerging markets is more subdued. overall, growth is low by historical standards. moreover, emerging markets are facing economic and financial risks: some are suffering from structural impediments and macroeconomic imbalances, while others have to adjust to lower commodity prices. they remain vulnerable to an abrupt shift in risk sentiment that could tighten financing conditions. a key issue is how emerging markets will be impacted by tighter financing conditions and the ensuing capital outflows, and to what extent this will have repercussions for euro area foreign demand. against this background, ensuring the continued resilience of the euro area economy is paramount. second, there are policy challenges related to our financial markets. the euro area financial system weathered several episodes of stress in the second half of last year. this is a sign that a lot has already been achieved with the establishment of banking union – which, however, is not complete yet. to make our financial system truly safe and sound, we need to progress in two main domains, which complement each other. on the one hand, we need to finalise and implement the work we started when establishing the single supervisory mechanism and the single resolution mechanism as the initial pillars of banking union. this includes further regulatory work to harmonise our rules for supervisory action and to ensure a consistent application of the bank recovery and resolution directive’s (brrd) bail-in provisions. on the other hand, we need a common public backstop for the single resolution fund to strengthen its credibility, and we need to ensure that confidence in the safety of deposits is equally high in all euro area member states by establishing a european deposit insurance scheme. ‘risk-reduction’ and ‘risk-sharing’ measures are two sides of the same coin and should be pursued in parallel: they are all essential to protecting the stability of the european banking sector. third, there are challenges related to the fiscal and economic policies of member states that require decisive policy action. fiscal policies should contribute to the economic recovery. at the same time, they should be in full compliance with the requirements of the stability and growth pact. this is important to maintain confidence in the european fiscal framework and in the sustainability of public finances. moreover, countries would benefit from a more growth-friendly composition of fiscal policies. this involves greater efficiency of public sector services and moving to a more growth-friendly tax system. but the ongoing cyclical recovery in the euro area should also be supported by effective structural policies, particularly actions to improve the business environment, including the provision of an adequate public infrastructure. such actions are vital to increase productive investment, boost job creation and raise productivity. if reforms are credible, carefully chosen and well designed, their positive effects can be felt quickly, particularly in the context of our supportive monetary policy stance. fourth and finally, there is still political uncertainty surrounding the european project. this is true in the broader context of our union. a solution that would anchor the united kingdom firmly within the eu while allowing the euro area to integrate further would boost confidence. the economic and monetary union architecture also remains an unfinished construction. citizens and markets are too often unsure about our capacity to act jointly in a spirit of common responsibility. we should prove them wrong. let me conclude and come back to the subject of our debate: your resolution on our annual report for 2014. let me assure you that we are reading this document closely. it reminds us of our duty as a public institution to conduct our business in a transparent and accountable manner. the publication of the diaries of members of the executive board that starts this month is only one example of this. i am looking forward to the debate and thank you for your attention.
vice-president of the commission.– mr president, first let me thank the rapporteur, mr marias, and his colleagues on the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ), for their work on this report. this ex-post assessment of the european central bank (ecb) activities by the european parliament is an important part of democratic accountability and a necessary complement to the ecb’s independence. the commission shares parliament’s view that the ecb’s independence, in the conduct of its monetary policy as enshrined in the treaties, is crucial to safeguard price stability. the monetary policy in the euro area is the exclusive competence of the ecb. with its monetary policy measures over the past years, including interest rate cuts, a series of targeted long-term refinancing operations and an expanded assets purchase programme, the ecb has acted to address the risks of an excessively long period of very low inflation. these measures include bank lending to the euro area non—financial private sector to help reduce financial fragmentation. they should support the economy and bring inflation closer to the ecb’s target of below, but close to, 2% over the medium term. the eu economy is continuing with a moderate recovery, and it is supported by certain tailwinds, such as low oil prices, the aforementioned accommodatory monetary policy and a correspondingly lower euro exchange rate, which is favourable for european exporters. at the same time we are also facing headwinds from geopolitical tensions in our neighbourhood – both our southern and eastern neighbourhoods – and from the slowdown in emerging markets. the global gdp growth forecast has also somewhat deteriorated. it is against this backdrop that we will be updating our economic forecast on thursday with our winter economic forecast. the commission fully shares parliament’s view that europe cannot only rely on monetary policy and a favourable external environment to lift gdp growth and to raise our economy’s growth potential. member states’ governments must roll up their sleeves and implement necessary structural reforms. structural, fiscal and monetary policies each have to play their role for a consistent, growth-friendly approach acting both on the demand and supply sides of our economies. on the fiscal side, adjustments undertaken in recent years have reduced deficits and stabilised debt levels in the euro area. but member states continue to face different fiscal challenges which call for a differentiated path of fiscal adjustment going forward. the commission agrees with the european parliament that fiscal adjustment, using the flexibility that is built into the rules of the stability and growth pact, needs to go hand in hand with the implementation of structural reforms: reforms of product, services and labour markets that increase productivity, help regain competitiveness, improve the business environment and reduce inequality. stimulating investment remains one of the commission’s policy priorities. the investment plan for europe will help to reverse recent downward trends in investment by supporting strategic projects and sme financing. european parliament support for a european fund for strategic investments initiative has been instrumental in laying the ground for decisive and swift union action to address the main investment needs in europe. with all the governance bodies in place since early january, efsi is now up and running. the take-up so far by the market and public authorities leaves us assured that we will meet the eur 315 billion investment target well within the three—year deadline. the commission also shares parliament’s view on the capital markets union. it is our common objective to support diversification of funding sources, promote cross-border investments and improve access to finance smes in particular. implementing the capital markets union action plan is an ambitious objective. the commission therefore counts on parliament’s strong support and commitment, in particular – but not only – for the upcoming legislative procedures. at the same time we agree with parliament that we must remain vigilant with regard to risks in all areas of the financial system arising in the current market situation. let me conclude by underlining that i see much common ground between your views and the commission’s. it is reassuring to know that we can count on your support in building the foundations for sustainable growth and job creation in europe. i thank you for your attention and look forward to a good and fruitful debate today.

in writing. ‒ the convention on long-range transboundary air pollution was signed in 1979 and entered into force in 1983. it has since been extended by eight protocols specifically identifying measures to be taken by the parties to reduce their emissions of air pollutants, including the aarhus protocol which in 1998 aimed to reduce and control anthropogenic emissions of lead, mercury and cadmium. i have approved this decision which aims to accept the amendments to that protocol in order to establish a higher level of protection of human health and the environment against transboundary air pollution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the parliament's resolution calling on the council to accept, on behalf of the european union, the 1998 amendment to the 1979 convention on long-range transboundary air pollution protocol on heavy metals. the aim of the protocol is to reduce and control anthropogenic emissions of heavy metals into the atmosphere, across borders and over long distances. it requires the parties to reduce their total annual emissions of lead, cadmium and mercury compared with the levels of these emissions in 1990 (or any other year between 1985 and 1995). the proposed amendment to the protocol aims to establish stricter emission limit values for dust emissions from certain large fixed sources as well as adaptive transitional provisions that will benefit future parties that accede to the protocol as amended between 1 january 2014 and 31 december 2019. this amendment should be transposed, in particular, by means of a directive setting new national emission ceilings for certain air pollutants and providing for an annual national emission inventory covering, inter alia, emissions of lead, cadmium and mercury.
in writing. the 1979 convention on long-range transboundary air pollution by heavy metals aims to protect the human environment from air pollution. such pollution may be characterized by the emission of heavy metals such as lead (pb), cadmium (cd) and mercury (hg) into the atmosphere. the aim of the protocol is therefore to reduce industrial emissions from the combustion and incineration of waste. but in view of the environmental problems these heavy metals can cause, it is appropriate (as the amendments emphasize) to reduce the mercury content of alkaline batteries and measuring devices and to keep an updated national inventory of pb, cd and hg emissions. the ratification of the amendments is an essential step towards a high level of protection of human health and the environment against transboundary air pollution.
in writing. ‒ in europe, air pollution is responsible for almost half a million premature deaths each year: parliament has therefore rightly updated its legislation on long-range transboundary air pollution, which is enshrined in a convention of the same name. this is particularly important to reduce and control emissions of heavy metals, which are a hazard in case of large or prolonged exposure, which can cause diseases and accelerated ageing. heavy metals are naturally present in our environment and used industrially, are released into the air as very fine particles and eventually fall back to the ground, contaminating the animals and plants we eat and eventually accumulating in our tissues. cadmium, found in pesticides and tv screens, and responsible for thousands of kidney cancers. lead, which is emitted by the metal industry and causes psychological disturbances, including saturnism. mercury, which is also produced in the production of electricity and is used in dental fillings, is considered by the who to be one of the ten chemicals of greatest concern to public health.
in writing. ‒ the convention on long-range transboundary air pollution aims to protect the human environment from air pollution. several studies conducted between 1972 and 1977 have shown that air pollutants can be transported thousands of kilometres before being precipitated. the problems of air pollution must therefore be tackled at international level. the convention established the framework for controlling and reducing the damage to human health and the environment caused by transboundary air pollution. to date, the convention has been extended by eight protocols specifically identifying measures to be taken by the parties to reduce their emissions of air pollutants. in december 2012, the protocol was amended by decisions 2012/5, 2012/6 and 2012/7. decision 2012/5 still needed to be ratified by the parties, as the amended protocol in particular sets stricter emission limit values for dust emissions from certain large fixed sources as well as flexible transitional provisions that will benefit future parties that will accede to the amended protocol before the end of 2019, including the countries of eastern and south-eastern europe. parliament approved this recommendation today.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the text and its amendments. the convention on long-range transboundary air pollution aims to protect the human environment from air pollution. several studies conducted between 1972 and 1977 have shown that air pollutants can be transported thousands of kilometres before being precipitated. the problems of air pollution must therefore be tackled at international level. the convention, which was signed in 1979 and entered into force in 1983, was the first international legally binding instrument in this field. it has established the framework for controlling and reducing the damage to human health and the environment caused by transboundary air pollution. it provides that the executive secretary of the united nations economic commission for europe shall provide its secretariat. the convention is implemented and monitored through the concerted programme for the monitoring and evaluation of the long-range transport of air pollutants in europe.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the parliament's resolution calling on the council to accept, on behalf of the european union, the amendments to the 1998 protocol to the 1979 convention on long-range transboundary air pollution on persistent organic pollutants. adopted in 1981, this convention is the main international legal framework governing cooperation and measures to limit and progressively reduce air pollution and to avoid its harmful effects on human health and the environment in the unece region. the text of the proposed amendments to the 1998 protocol includes new substances, an update of the proposed regime for certain emissions and the limit values (levs) for dioxins/furans (pcdd/fs) emissions from certain waste incinerators, the establishment of new limit values for pcdd/fs emissions from agglomeration workshops and electric arc furnaces, and the addition of pcbs to the list of substances whose annual emissions must remain below the level of the reference year and be reported. i support and welcome this news to better protect human health and the environment.
air pollution does not stop at the border. often, this pollution travels many miles before it hits far away. it is therefore necessary to address the problems caused by air pollution internationally and across borders. in 1983 a convention with a legally binding instrument to limit the environmental and health effects of transboundary air pollution entered into force for the first time. in recent years, a number of protocols have been added to the existing convention to allow a more efficient approach to environmental problems. the latest amendment adds a series of harmful substances to which the implementing rules, emission limit values and reporting obligations will apply. i hope that by ratifying these amendments we will take another step towards better protection of air quality and public health against transboundary air pollution.
in writing. ‒ on tuesday, the european parliament approved a tightening of its air quality legislation. more specifically, it is an amendment to the geneva convention on long-range transboundary air pollution which strengthens the fight against persistent organic pollutants such as aldrin, chlordane, heptachlore, mirex and toxaphene. under these barbaric titles are the infamous "pops", dangerous chemical compounds that have in common toxicity, persistence in the environment, long-distance transport and bio-amplification, i.e. the fact that the concentration increases in the food chain. they are found in pesticides, in pcbs added to paints and plastics, and in the combustion of wood and household waste, especially in the form of dioxins. the legislative amendment aims to add seven new substances to the list limiting the use of persistent organic pollutants and to update some existing schemes. i welcome this adjustment, especially since at the same time a similar vote was on the restriction of heavy metals.

in writing. ‒ the primary objective of the platform is to add value at union level to the efforts of member states and union institutions to effectively tackle the complex problem of undeclared work and to address its multiple implications and consequences, including by encouraging and promoting undeclared work through appropriate policies. these policies are all the more necessary in the light of the recent findings of the eurofound study, which highlight a strong correlation between the size and growth of the underground economy and austerity policies, which result in draconian budget cuts, increased deregulation and a significant reduction in the role of the state. the urgency of the measures to be taken cannot be underestimated in view of the multiple and very negative consequences of undeclared work: severe exploitation situations, precarious living and working conditions for millions of workers across the union, clear unfair competition that severely disrupts the single market and heavy losses for member states' budgets and social security systems.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution establishing a 'european platform' to strengthen cooperation between the ministries of labour, trade unions and employers' associations of the member states to combat undeclared work. at present, undeclared work accounts for an average of 18% of eu gdp. for workers, undeclared work too often means dangerous working conditions and low wages, which fosters social dumping, particularly in crossborder work. the purpose of this platform should thus be, firstly, to prevent, discourage and combat undeclared work, but also to promote the transformation of such activities into declared work, and, secondly, to encourage practical, effective and efficient cross-border actions, and to develop a reliable and effective system for the rapid exchange of information between national bodies. this should not, however, interfere with member states' own measures or seek to harmonise the regulatory systems of the different eu countries.
